Question: How does cannabis impede a person’s logic capabilities?
Answer: Huh. I’ve read the answers so far, and other than the one that says “it doesn’t,” they generally don’t answer the question. So, with full recognition that this is subjective, anecdotal, and completely unscientific, and may not generalize to the population as a whole: In my experience, yes, first of all, it absolutely can and does impede logic capabilities. Specifically, in my experience: Put together, this suggests that the part of the brain responsible for fluent language production gets impaired. It feels similar to a mild form of conduction aphasia, or rather a conduction alexia: I know what I’m trying to express but something happens in the process of getting from intention to words. This is accompanied by a tendency to get lost in the middle of a sentence, so I have to restart from the beginning, which is kind of in the same general lexical malfunction area. I also find my sense of time is severely distorted—everything seems to slow down, and I’ll find myself thinking everything is taking forever to happen around me, which causes me to second-guess word choices while I’m writing. This isn’t purely subjective—I can see it in what I’ve written the next day (and it’s one of the reasons I don’t particularly like being high). I also experience promiscuous pattern recognition: I’ll have the subjective experience that the world is opening up and I’m seeing connections between things I can’t normally see…but then, if I write them down, I’ll generally find that those connections that seemed so clear while I was high are actually spurious. This is a logical error called apophenia, and it’s a common cognitive error among conspiracy nutters. In fact, while I don’t know of any research that backs this up, I would not be at all surprised if drug-induced apophenia turns out to be why some cannabis users experience paranoia when they’re high. Apophenia is a known component of paranoid schizophrenia and some forms of psychosis.

Name: Franklin Veaux
Question: Do you think that we Need laws that explicitly state that AI Platforms cannot train on copyrighted material without consent of the copyright holders, to clear up the current legal ambiguities surrounding this matter? Why or why not?
Answer: Yes, I absolutely do. I think a case can be made that copyrighted work is not available to be used to train AI without permission, though this is an edge case not explicitly part of the law. Several high profile copyright cases are already pending against Midjourney, OpenAI, and others that will with luck shed some light on this particular dark corner of IP law. Nobody has yet (to my knowledge) sued the end users of AI systems for trademark or copyright violation, but it’s going to happen, I’d bet money on it. Explicit legal guidelines about use of copyrighted material to train AI systems really needs to be written.
